Archive item 4: Survey Report – Pauri Range Habitat Assessment
Source format: Survey report

KUMAON WILDLIFE TRUST
Field Survey Report – Pauri Range Habitat Assessment
Report No. KWT/S02/2025-08
Period of Survey: 15 February 2025 – 20 August 2025
Submitted to: Wildlife Institute of India (WII), Dehradun
Prepared by: Field Survey Team, Kumaon Wildlife Trust, Nainital

1. INTRODUCTION
Pauri Range (hereafter "the Range"), located in the Kosi River catchment, Pauri block, Nainital District, was surveyed as part of the ongoing corridor assessment under the Kumaon Wildlife Trust's habitat monitoring programme. The survey aimed to document current vegetation status, wildlife presence through sign surveys, and the condition of water sources across the Range. This report consolidates data collected over six months, covering both the late dry season and the early monsoon period.

2. SURVEY AREA
The Range comprises approximately 1250 hectares of mixed forest and scrubland. The KWT site survey S02 reports that Pauri Range area_hectares is 1250 hectares. Record status: current. This figure is current as of the 2024–25 fiscal year and is used as the baseline for all density calculations in this report. The area is bounded by the Kosi River to the south, agricultural land to the east, and revenue forest to the north and west. Elevation ranges from 620 m to 1,140 m above mean sea level.

3. METHODOLOGY
3.1 Vegetation Plots
A total of 24 permanent vegetation plots (10 m × 10 m for trees, 5 m × 5 m for shrubs) were established using a stratified random design. Grid coordinates were recorded using a handheld GPS unit (accuracy ±5 m). Plot locations were selected to represent three habitat types: dense mixed forest (DMF), open scrubland (OSL), and riparian woodland (RWL). Each plot was visited twice during the survey period – once in the pre-monsoon season (February–April) and once in the early monsoon (June–August).

3.2 Sign Surveys
Transect walks were conducted along existing animal trails and forest roads. A total of 18 transects, each 1–2 km in length, were walked twice per month. Signs recorded included pugmarks, scat, scratch marks, feeding signs, and direct sightings. Species codes were assigned as per the KWT field manual.

3.3 Water Source Checks
All perennial and seasonal water sources within the Range were mapped and monitored. A total of 11 water sources were identified: 7 perennial springs, 3 seasonal pools, and 1 stream segment of the Kosi River. Each source was visited monthly to record water presence, depth, turbidity, and signs of wildlife use.

4. RESULTS
4.1 Vegetation Plots
A total of 38 tree species and 47 shrub/herb species were recorded across the 24 plots. The most common tree species were Sal (Shorea robusta), Rohini (Mallotus philippensis), and Amaltas (Cassia fistula). The dense mixed forest plots showed the highest species richness, with an average of 18 tree species per plot. Open scrubland plots were dominated by Lantana camara and Carissa spinarum. Riparian woodland plots had a distinct assemblage, including Jamun (Syzygium cumini) and Hald (Adina cordifolia).

The pre-monsoon survey recorded an average canopy cover of 62% in DMF plots, 28% in OSL plots, and 45% in RWL plots. Early monsoon data showed a slight increase in canopy cover (average 65% in DMF) due to leaf flush. Regeneration counts (seedlings and saplings) were highest in RWL plots, with an average of 14 individuals per plot, and lowest in OSL plots (average 4 per plot).

4.2 Sign Surveys
A total of 214 sign encounters were recorded across all transects during the survey period. The most frequently recorded signs were of Chital (Axis axis) and Sambar (Rusa unicolor), with 68 and 52 encounters respectively. Wild boar (Sus scrofa) signs were recorded 31 times. Carnivore signs were less common: Leopard (Panthera pardus) pugmarks were recorded on 12 occasions, and Jungle Cat (Felis chaus) scat on 9 occasions.

Direct sightings were rare. A single sighting of a Leopard was reported on 22 March 2025 near grid coordinate 29.8312°N, 78.9124°E. A troop of Rhesus Macaque (Macaca mulatta) was seen on multiple occasions at the eastern boundary. No evidence of Tiger (Panthera tigris) was recorded during the survey period, although local villagers reported hearing a large cat call in April 2025.

- Species sightings recorded: 31 confirmed sightings, including 2 leopard, 5 Himalayan goral, and 24 other mammal and bird species.  
- Patrols conducted: 14 joint patrols with Forest Department staff.  
- Community meetings held: 9 meetings in villages adjacent to the Pauri Range.  

These figures are preliminary and subject to final verification. A detailed report will be circulated by 15/10/2025.  

I thank all staff for their cooperation and look forward to the next season.

documents.title: Field Log – Pauri Range Daily Observations
documents.content:
**12/01/2025 (Sunday)**

05:50 – Early start. Overcast, drizzle started at 06:10. Patrol route: Kosi River east bank to Bamrauli village boundary.

08:15 – Found snare (wire loop) near a known deer trail, approx 1.5 km from Bamrauli. Snare was old, rusted, not set. Removed and logged. Coordinates: 29.873N, 78.612E.

09:40 – Met village forest committee member at Bamrauli. He reported a leopard sighting on 10 Jan evening, near the village cattle shed. No attack, but villagers are worried. Gave him our contact number.

11:00 – Continued patrol. Rain stopped. Visibility good.

13:30 – Lunch at Bamrauli primary school verandah. Ramesh Negi spoke with a local farmer about crop raiding. Farmer said wild boar damaged his potato patch last week.

15:00 – Return patrol via Kosi River west bank. Saw 2 grey langur troops, no other mammals.

16:30 – Back at base. Weather: drizzle on/off, max temp 15°C. Logged snare removal in SNARE REGISTER (entry #14).

Note: Ramesh Negi's field notes for today are in Kumaoni; he says it is easier for him to record details in his mother tongue. Per his notes, the leopard sighting was near the "pipal tree at the east edge of the cattle shed." He also noted the farmer's name as "Lal Singh" and the potato field location as "the one with the broken fence."

---

**15/01/2025 (Wednesday)**

06:00 – Clear sky, cold. Temp 6°C at base.

06:30 – Patrol route: Chidiyapur ridge to Kosi River bend (reverse of 10 Jan). Foot patrol, 4 km.

08:00 – Fresh tiger pugmarks on the ridge trail, heading south towards the river. Pugmark size: 12 cm (hind paw). Age: likely from last night. Ramesh Negi confirmed – he said the edges were still sharp.

08:45 – Followed pugmarks for 500 m. Lost them on rocky ground near the river.

10:00 – Checked camera trap CT-08 (ridge trail). Camera had been triggered 3 times overnight. Downloaded photos. Photos show a large male tiger walking past at 23:40 on 14 Jan. Clear images. This is the first tiger photo from CT-08 this season.

11:30 – Radioed base. Informed Dr. Rao. She asked to keep the location confidential for now.

13:00 – Lunch at Chidiyapur patrol hut. Ramesh Negi said the tiger is the same one we saw pugmarks of in December (larger left hind toe). He recognized the pattern.

Field notes S03 record that Ramesh Negi's field_notes_language is Kumaoni. Record status: current.

14:00 – Continued patrol to Kosi River crossing. No further sign. River level still low.

16:00 – Back at base. Logged tiger sighting in TIGER LOG (entry #3). Weather: clear, max temp 17°C.

Note: All field notes for this patrol were written in Kumaoni by Ramesh Negi. He prefers this for detailed tracking observations. The notes are on file.

---

**18/01/2025 (Saturday)**

05:40 – Light rain. Delayed start by 30 min.

06:30 – Patrol route: Kosi River west bank to Bamrauli village boundary (south side).

08:10 – Found fresh elephant tracks near the river, heading north. Two adults, one calf. Tracks approx 2 hours old. Followed for 1 km, then lost them in the river.

09:30 – Camera trap CT-11 (near river ford) had been knocked over. Re-set it. SD card was empty – camera must have been triggered by the elephants and the card was full. Replaced card. Battery at 60%.

11:00 – Reached Bamrauli. Met with Lal Singh (the farmer from 12 Jan). He said the leopard was seen again on 16 Jan, near the same cattle shed. No attack. He requested we do a night patrol.

12:30 – Lunch at Bamrauli. Ramesh Negi spoke with the village headman. The headman said the villagers are willing to help with patrolling if we provide torches.

14:00 – Return patrol. No further sightings.

16:00 – Back at base. Weather: drizzle, max temp 14°C.

Note: Night patrol planned for 20 Jan. Will coordinate with village volunteers.

---

**20/01/2025 (Monday)**

18:00 – Night patrol started. Team: Ramesh Negi, Mahesh (helper), 2 village volunteers. Route: Bamrauli cattle shed to Chidiyapur ridge.

19:30 – Positioned at cattle shed. No leopard activity until 21:00.

documents.title: Survey Report – Pauri Range Habitat Assessment
documents.content:
KUMAON WILDLIFE TRUST
Field Survey Report – Pauri Range Habitat Assessment
Report No. KWT/S02/2025-08
Period of Survey: 15 February 2025 – 20 August 2025
Submitted to: Wildlife Institute of India (WII), Dehradun
Prepared by: Field Survey Team, Kumaon Wildlife Trust, Nainital

1. INTRODUCTION
Pauri Range (hereafter "the Range"), located in the Kosi River catchment, Pauri block, Nainital District, was surveyed as part of the ongoing corridor assessment under the Kumaon Wildlife Trust's habitat monitoring programme. The survey aimed to document current vegetation status, wildlife presence through sign surveys, and the condition of water sources across the Range. This report consolidates data collected over six months, covering both the late dry season and the early monsoon period.

2. SURVEY AREA
The Range comprises approximately 1250 hectares of mixed forest and scrubland. The KWT site survey S02 reports that Pauri Range area_hectares is 1250 hectares. Record status: current. This figure is current as of the 2024–25 fiscal year and is used as the baseline for all density calculations in this report. The area is bounded by the Kosi River to the south, agricultural land to the east, and revenue forest to the north and west. Elevation ranges from 620 m to 1,140 m above mean sea level.

3. METHODOLOGY
3.1 Vegetation Plots
A total of 24 permanent vegetation plots (10 m × 10 m for trees, 5 m × 5 m for shrubs) were established using a stratified random design. Grid coordinates were recorded using a handheld GPS unit (accuracy ±5 m). Plot locations were selected to represent three habitat types: dense mixed forest (DMF), open scrubland (OSL), and riparian woodland (RWL). Each plot was visited twice during the survey period – once in the pre-monsoon season (February–April) and once in the early monsoon (June–August).

3.2 Sign Surveys
Transect walks were conducted along existing animal trails and forest roads. A total of 18 transects, each 1–2 km in length, were walked twice per month. Signs recorded included pugmarks, scat, scratch marks, feeding signs, and direct sightings. Species codes were assigned as per the KWT field manual.

3.3 Water Source Checks
All perennial and seasonal water sources within the Range were mapped and monitored. A total of 11 water sources were identified: 7 perennial springs, 3 seasonal pools, and 1 stream segment of the Kosi River. Each source was visited monthly to record water presence, depth, turbidity, and signs of wildlife use.

4. RESULTS
4.1 Vegetation Plots
A total of 38 tree species and 47 shrub/herb species were recorded across the 24 plots. The most common tree species were Sal (Shorea robusta), Rohini (Mallotus philippensis), and Amaltas (Cassia fistula). The dense mixed forest plots showed the highest species richness, with an average of 18 tree species per plot. Open scrubland plots were dominated by Lantana camara and Carissa spinarum. Riparian woodland plots had a distinct assemblage, including Jamun (Syzygium cumini) and Hald (Adina cordifolia).

The pre-monsoon survey recorded an average canopy cover of 62% in DMF plots, 28% in OSL plots, and 45% in RWL plots. Early monsoon data showed a slight increase in canopy cover (average 65% in DMF) due to leaf flush. Regeneration counts (seedlings and saplings) were highest in RWL plots, with an average of 14 individuals per plot, and lowest in OSL plots (average 4 per plot).

4.2 Sign Surveys
A total of 214 sign encounters were recorded across all transects during the survey period. The most frequently recorded signs were of Chital (Axis axis) and Sambar (Rusa unicolor), with 68 and 52 encounters respectively. Wild boar (Sus scrofa) signs were recorded 31 times. Carnivore signs were less common: Leopard (Panthera pardus) pugmarks were recorded on 12 occasions, and Jungle Cat (Felis chaus) scat on 9 occasions.

Direct sightings were rare. A single sighting of a Leopard was reported on 22 March 2025 near grid coordinate 29.8312°N, 78.9124°E. A troop of Rhesus Macaque (Macaca mulatta) was seen on multiple occasions at the eastern boundary. No evidence of Tiger (Panthera tigris) was recorded during the survey period, although local villagers reported hearing a large cat call in April 2025.
